A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PoE-World study. Text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable matching of the equations, figures, tables, appendices, and checklist despite their reordered placement.

before.justification: v3 reports original agent scores, prediction accuracies, hard-constraint ablations, and PPO pretraining results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 5–6.

after.justification: v4 retains the original experimental results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 5–6, including agent performance and world-model prediction measurements.

M1.justification: Sections 3 and A.1–A.2 retain the same programmatic-expert representation, synthesis and weight-optimization procedure, pruning, hard constraints, and hierarchical planner.

E1.justification: Both versions use Pong, Montezuma’s Revenge, and their alternative environments with the same task requirements and object-centric observations. No training or evaluation coverage is added or removed.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain the same Random Agent, PPO, ReAct, and WorldCoder comparators. The added LMAct bibliography entry does not introduce an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The demonstration budgets, 1000-frame prediction tests, evaluation metrics, PPO training budgets, frame skipping, and planning procedures are unchanged in Section 4 and Appendices A.2–A.4.

E4.justification: The hard-constraint ablation in Table 4, PPO pretraining comparison in Figure 6, and qualitative comparison of learned world models remain unchanged. No supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both retain the checklist statement that error bars are computed over five seeds, the same planner-repeat information in Appendix A.2, and identical uncertainty displays.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4, Figures 5–6, and the qualitative findings are unchanged. For example, Table 1 retains PoE-World + Planner scores of −12.33 ± 0.88 on Pong and 100 ± 0.00 on Montezuma’s Revenge.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), the conditional-independence assumptions, history-based formulation, and constraint and multi-timestep definitions are unchanged. Neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same claims about sample-efficient symbolic world modeling, compositional generalization, scalability, and use for planning and RL pretraining.

C2.justification: The interpretations of hard constraints and compositionality remain identical, as do the limitations concerning symbolic inputs, exploration, reward learning, and planning efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1–A.5 retain the same LLM version, prompts, hyperparameters, implementation details, hardware, costs, execution times, and code-access information. Their relocation adds no reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v4 adds Ruoss et al.’s LMAct: A benchmark for in-context imitation learning with long multimodal demonstrations as reference [76]. The related-work discussion and research positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v4 places the appendix before the NeurIPS Paper Checklist, reversing their order in v3. Otherwise, the prose is unchanged apart from the version stamp and consequential citation renumbering.

P2.justification: Appendix Tables 5–10 and Figure 7 move with the appendix, retaining their content, captions, and within-page layout. The added reference slightly expands the bibliography layout; the main figures and tables are visually identical.

improvement.justification: v4 moves the unchanged appendix ahead of the checklist and adds an LMAct bibliography entry without integrating it into the discussion. Methods, evidence, explanations, and reproducibility information are preserved, so these limited editorial changes produce no meaningful net difference in overall quality.
